title: 「落選したら絶対出ない」田中眞紀子氏が政界引退の理由を明かす…選挙制度に持論も展開「筆記試験と立会演説会を」
extracted_text: 元外務大臣の田中眞紀子氏と新潟県出身のジャーナリスト・風間晋氏との対談が3月中旬に東京都内で行われた。高市早苗総理大臣と当選同期の田中眞紀子氏だが、2012年の衆院選で敗れ、政界から引退した。対談の中で語ったのは、「落選したら絶対に出ない」と決めていた理由、そして今の政治への率直な思いだった。 当選同期には、高市早苗総理大臣や野田聖子元総務大臣などがいる。幼いころから田中角栄元総理の姿を見ていた眞紀子氏が政治家になるのは必然だった。 風間氏が眞紀子氏に「政治家になった理由」を問うと、眞紀子氏は「国を良くしたいんですよ。国を良くしたい。それから、恵まれてない人たちをいっぱい見ているから。みんなお互いに1回しかない人生を良くしてあげたい。そのために私が何ができるか」と政治家を志した理由について語った。 幼少期から様々な大物政治家と面会していた眞紀子氏にとって、政治の世界は身近なもので「異質な世界ではなかった」という。 「科学技術庁長官のとき、国会で野党の議員からガンガン質問された後、その先生がすーっと来て『大臣、大変だったな。俺、親父にすごく世話になったんだよ』と。別の資料をくれて『これ、勉強しといたほうがいいから』って。結構みんな良くしてくださった。2代目の得があったんです、すごく。だから国会議員生活は楽しかった」 国会が終わった後には、多くの同僚議員などに誘われて会食をして情報収集にも勤しんだという。その後、小泉政権で外務大臣を務め、民主党に入党後には文部科学大臣を歴任。衆院議員を6期務めた。 しかし、政権交代がなされる2012年の衆院選で眞紀子氏は自民党候補に敗れ、議席を失った。そして、政界から引退した。 「選挙で落とされたら絶対に出ないと決めていたから。落選というのは、有権者が『他の方が良かった』と判断したんだから。その判断を尊重する。1回負けても、次また出る人が多いが、私は出ないと決めていた」 国会では、議員定数削減に向けて衆議院の選挙制度の在り方を検討する与野党の協議会が開かれているが、眞紀子氏は現在の選挙制度に異を唱える。 「選挙制度を変えて、議員の数も減らして。私、時々言うんだけど、筆記試験はどうですか。最低限の歴史とか外交の問題とか、基本的なことが分かっているか。あとは父の頃にやっていた立会演説会。候補者がみんな集まって、有権者が聞きに行く。質問を投げて、それに答えさせる。そうすると、意味が分かってない人もいるし、しどろもどろになる人もいる。それを見て、有権者が選べるじゃないですか」 もう一度、政界復帰する可能性がないか尋ねると「年齢制限でダメ。50代だったら出るでしょうけどね」と笑って答えた眞紀子氏。一方で、「今の状態でじっとしていたらいけない」とも語る。 政治家の娘として生まれ、政治の世界を見続けてきた眞紀子氏の言葉は今の日本政治そのものに問いを突きつけている。
translated_text: A dialogue between former Foreign Minister Tanaka Makiko and journalist Kazama Shin from Niigata Prefecture was held in Tokyo in mid-March. Tanaka Makiko was elected to the same Diet class as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, but she was defeated in the 2012 Lower House election and retired from politics. In the dialogue, she explained why she had decided never to return if she lost an election, and shared her candid thoughts about current politics. Her fellow newbies elected at the same time include Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and former Internal Affairs Minister Seiko Noda. For Makiko, who grew up watching former Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka, becoming a politician was almost inevitable. When asked why she became a politician, Makiko replied: "I wanted to make the country better. I wanted to improve the country. And I saw many people who weren't fortunate. I wanted to help everyone make the most of their one and only life. That's what motivated me to become a politician." For Makiko, who met various senior politicians from childhood, the world of politics was never an alien environment. "When I was Science and Technology Agency Director, I got peppered with questions from opposition lawmakers in the Diet. Then that senior member would quietly come up to me and say, 'Minister, that was tough, wasn't it? My father really owed you a favor.' Then he'd give me other materials and say, 'You should study this.' People were really kind to me. I gained a lot from my two terms. So my life as a Diet member was enjoyable." After Diet sessions, she was often invited to dinners by fellow lawmakers to gather information. She later served as Foreign Minister under the Koizumi administration, and after joining the Democratic Party of Japan, served as Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Minister. She served six terms as a Lower House member. However, in the 2012 Lower House election following the change of government, Makiko was defeated by a Liberal Democratic Party candidate and lost her seat, retiring from politics. "I decided that if I lost an election, I would absolutely not run again. Losing an election means voters decided someone else was better. I respect that decision. Many people run again after losing once, but I decided I wouldn't." In the Diet, a cross-party working group has been discussing the structure of Lower House electoral districts to reduce the number of seats, but Makiko disagrees with the current system. "Change the electoral system and reduce the number of lawmakers. I sometimes suggest: how about a written test? To check if they have at least a basic understanding of history and diplomacy. Also, the campaign rallies that were held in my father's time, where all candidates gather and voters go to listen. Voters can ask questions and get answers. Then you can see who understands the issues and who gets flustered. Voters can make their choice." When asked if there's any possibility of a political comeback, she laughed and replied, "I'm disqualified by the age limit. If I were in my 50s, I'd run." However, she also said, "If I just stay quiet in the current situation, that wouldn't be right." The words of Makiko, born as a politician's daughter who has continuously observed the political world, pose a question to Japanese politics today.
title_en: Tanaka Makiko Explains Retirement Reason: 'If I Lose an Election, I Will Absolutely Not Run Again' ... Proposes Election Reform Ideas Including Written Tests and Campaign Rallies
